title: Det. No. 23-0051, 45 WTD 044 (2026)
description: Two marijuana retailers protest the Department’s assessments to the extent the Department disallowed [exemptions] for sales of marijuana to customers made prior to the issuance of the customers’ patient recognition card ID numbers. Taxpayers contend that their point-of-sale software did not maintain a copy of the original ID number when customers got new recognition cards with new ID numbers. While marijuana products can be exempt from taxation under RCW 82.08.9998, Taxpayers did not follow the recordkeeping requirements. We deny the petition.

RCW 82.08.9998: EXEMPTIONS – RECORD KEEPING REQUIREMENTS
FOR CANNABIS PRODUCTS EXEMPTION. The legislature explicitly granted
the Department the authority to determine the “information establishing eligibility
for the exemption” a taxpayer must maintain to qualify for this exemption. The
Department established those criteria for in a special notice issued May 6, 2016.
Headnotes are provided as a convenience for the reader and are not in any way a part of the decision
or in any way to be used in construing or interpreting this Determination.
Kelly, T.R.O. – Two marijuana1 retailers protest the Department’s assessments to the extent the
Department disallowed [exemptions] for sales of marijuana to customers made prior to the
issuance of the customers’ patient recognition card ID numbers. Taxpayers contend that their
point-of-sale software did not maintain a copy of the original ID number when customers got new
recognition cards with new ID numbers. While marijuana products can be exempt from taxation
under RCW 82.08.9998, Taxpayers did not follow the recordkeeping requirements. We deny the
petition.2
ISSUES
Have Taxpayers provided the Department with suitable records under WAC 458-20-254 (Rule
254) to prove certain sales of marijuana products are exempt from retail sales tax under RCW
82.08.9998?
FINDINGS OF FACT
[Taxpayer] doing business as [Entity 1] and [Entity 2] (referred to as Taxpayers) are affiliated
entities operating as recreational and medical marijuana retailers selling marijuana products and
paraphernalia . . . .
1 The term “marijuana” was the statutory term for the entirety of the audit period. Through SSHB 1210, Chapter 16,
Laws of 2022 (effective June 9, 2022), the [l]egislature replaced the term “marijuana” with the term “cannabis.”
2
Identifying details regarding the taxpayer and the assessment have been redacted pursuant to RCW 82.32.410.

Det. No. 23-0051, 45 WTD 044 (May 5, 2026) 45
The Department of Revenue’s (Department’s) Audit Division (Audit) inspected both Taxpayers’
records for the period of January 1, 2018, through June 30, 2021 (Audit Period).
Taxpayers possess medical cannabis endorsements. This allows Taxpayers to make sales tax
exempt sales of qualifying products to customers with qualifying patient recognition cards.
Audit reviewed Taxpayers’ records to verify the sales to customers with qualifying patient
recognition cards.
Taxpayers did not retain copies of customers’ patient recognition cards. Instead, Taxpayers’
[point-of-sale system] retained reports containing records of individual transactions and associated
patient recognition card ID numbers.
Audit compared the provided ID Numbers to the Department of Health’s database. This process
revealed several issues including (1) sales of non-qualifying marijuana paraphernalia products, (2)
sales to ID Numbers that were expired at the time of sale, (3) and sales to ID Numbers prior to
their date of issuance. Audit came to understand that instead of creating a new profile for a
customer when that customer received a new ID Number, Taxpayers overrode that customer’s
prior number with the new one. This resulted in the point-of-sale system not retaining the prior ID
Number. As Taxpayers retained no documentation, these sales were disallowed.
On May 27, 2022, Audit issued [Letter 1] to [Entity 1] for a total of $. . . .3
On May 27, 2022, Audit issued [Letter 2] to [Entity 2] for a total of $. . . .4
Taxpayers timely filed petitions for administrative review. Subsequently, Taxpayers clarified that
they were not contesting the adjustments to the extent that they related to sales of non-qualifying
marijuana paraphernalia products or sales to ID Numbers that were expired at the time of sale.
Taxpayers are only contesting the adjustments to the extent they relate to sales made prior to
medical card issuance. Taxpayers contend that the original ID Number data had been overridden
but valid records existed at the time of sale.
Taxpayers made repeated attempts to get more detailed information from [point-of-sale system]
with limited results. Eventually Taxpayers provided additional records to bolster their argument,
including a spreadsheet prepared by [point-of-sale system] showing ID Numbers, point-of-sale
device identification, receipt numbers, dates of sale, employee names, patient names when
available, and other transaction detail.
Audit reviewed the information but did not believe it warranted adjustment to the assessments. As
the new information did not contain any old ID Numbers that might have been overridden, Audit
concluded the new records did not resolve the issue of sales to ID Numbers prior to their date of
issuance.
3 This comprised $. . . in adjusted sales and use tax, $. . . in disallowed deductions to sales and use tax, and $. . . in

Det. No. 23-0051, 45 WTD 044 (May 5, 2026) 46
ANALYSIS
Washington requires persons making retail sales to collect and remit retail sales tax unless an
exemption applies. RCW 82.08.020; RCW 82.08.050. “Retail sale” is statutorily defined and
includes the sale of tangible personal property. RCW 82.04.050(1)(a). “Tangible personal
property” means property that can be “seen, weighed, measured, felt, or touched . . . .” WAC 458-
20-193(1)(c). Generally, the sale of marijuana is a retail sale subject to retail sales tax as tangible
property. Accordingly, Taxpayer must remit retail sales tax for retail sales and pay retailing
business and occupation (B&O) tax on its gross proceeds of sales unless an exemption applies.
RCW 82.08.020; RCW 82.04.250.
The legislature provides an exemption from retail sales tax for the sale of certain marijuana
products by marijuana retailers with marijuana endorsements to qualifying patients or designated
providers who have been issued recognition cards. RCW 82.08.9998(1)(a). Taxpayers are
marijuana retailers with a medical marijuana endorsement. Because RCW 82.08.9998 provides an
exemption from a prescribed tax, we construe its application narrowly. See Budget Rent-A-Car,
Inc. v. Dep’t of Revenue, 81, Wn.2d 171, 500 P.2d 764 (1972); Det. No 01-007, 20 WTD 214, 231
(2001) (stating the Department construes exemptions narrowly in favor of taxation). Additionally,
the taxpayer has the burden to prove the right to any exemption from taxation. See Det. No. 19-
0185R, 40 WTD 231, 234 (2021).
RCW 82.08.9998 includes the requirements to claim the exemption. Namely, “Each seller making
exempt sales under subsection (1) of this section must maintain information establishing eligibility
for the exemption in the form and manner required by the department.” RCW 82.08.9998. In RCW
82.08.9998, the “department” refers to the Department of Revenue. See RCW 82.02.010(2). In
RCW 82.08.9998(2), the legislature explicitly granted the Department the authority to determine
the “information establishing eligibility for the exemption” a taxpayer must maintain.
Every taxpayer “must” keep and preserve, for a period of five years, “suitable records” as may be
necessary to determine the tax for which taxpayer is liable. RCW 82.32.070(1). WAC 458-20-254
is the Department’s administrative rule detailing recordkeeping [and] explains further what
suitable records must be kept. With regards to exemptions, the taxpayer must keep “complete and
adequate records” to demonstrate the amounts of all exemptions claimed “through supporting
records or documentation required by statute or administrative rule, or other supporting records or
documentation necessary to substantiate” the deduction. Rule 254(3)(a)(ii). RCW 82.08.9998(2)
does not contain specific requirements but states the seller “must maintain information establishing
eligibility for the exemption in the form and manner required by the department.”
The Department clarified what information taxpayers must maintain for the retail sales and use tax
exemption for marijuana retailers with a medical endorsement by issuing a Special Notice on May
6, 2016 (Special Notice). In addition to the fact that the Special Notice predates the Audit Period,
it explicitly states it is intended for marijuana retailers with a medical endorsement, like Taxpayers.
Special Notice, p. 1. [The Department stated, u]nder the section titled “How do I document these
exemptions?” . . . :

Det. No. 23-0051, 45 WTD 044 (May 5, 2026) 47
Retailers must:
• Verify the qualifying patient or designated provider has a current recognition
card.
• Enter the qualifying patient or designated provider’s recognition card number
into LCB’s traceability system.
• Keep a copy of the qualifying patient or designated provider’s recognition card
as required by RCW 69.50.375[(3)](e). Retailers only need to keep one copy of
each valid recognition card and do not need to get multiple copies of the same
card for repeat customers.
• Keep records of tax exempt sales, including the applicable recognition card
number used by the purchaser, for at least five years.
Id. at 3. Taxpayers must satisfy every requirement in the notice.
In the instant case, Taxpayers fail two separate requirements, each of which individually would be
sufficient to deny the petition.
First, Taxpayers failed to keep a copy of the qualifying patient or designated provider’s recognition
cards. Taxpayers were required to keep copies of these cards and not merely equivalent
information under the Special Notice. While Taxpayers provided records to include ID Numbers,
point-of-sale device identification, receipt numbers, dates of sale, employee names, patient names
when available, and other transaction detail, Taxpayers did not provide copies of actual cards.
Second, Taxpayers failed the last requirement. In overriding ID Numbers in their . . . point-of-sale
system, Taxpayers lost any records of applicable ID Numbers they had accepted for the sales.
While Taxpayers worked with [point-of-sale system] to prepare a spreadsheet, Taxpayers were
unable to retrieve any of this specific data. Taxpayers were required to keep this data for five years.
Taxpayers failed to do so, and Taxpayers’ records instead only contain records of sales to ID
Numbers prior to their date of issuance. Such records do not satisfy the recordkeeping requirement.
Taxpayers hold the burden to prove the right to any exemption. It is not the Department’s burden
or responsibility to verify tax exempt sales beyond Taxpayers’ records. Because Taxpayers cannot
verify tax exempt sales, Audit properly denied the exemption.
DECISION AND DISPOSITION
We deny Taxpayers’ petition.
Dated this 13th day of March 2023.
